title: Trump and Xi Meet at White House: AI, Trade, Taiwan, and Iran on the Table
summary:
For the first time in more than 10 years, a Chinese leader visited Washington. President Trump hosted Xi Jinping at the White House on Thursday, welcoming him with a military review on the South Lawn. The two held two meetings and delivered remarks, though a dispute over press access — CNN and MS NOW correspondents were briefly barred before being readmitted — played out during the public portion of the visit. A state dinner followed Thursday evening.

So what was actually on the agenda? According to Nick Schifrin of the PBS NewsHour, four topics topped the list: trade, technology, Taiwan, and Iran.

On trade, the U.S. and China agreed to extend what they call a trade truce. The U.S. will not raise tariffs on Beijing, and China will continue exporting rare earth magnets — crucial components in everything from cell phones to electric vehicles to F-35 fighter jets. China has a near monopoly on heavy rare earths. U.S. officials are also considering narrow tariff cuts on non-strategic goods like fireworks and low-end consumer products.

Technology was next. Beijing has long complained about American export controls on semiconductors, but U.S. officials say there is no interest in easing those. There is, however, interest in discussing artificial intelligence. The two countries are launching a U.S.-China AI Dialogue, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed a dedicated communications line to report national security AI incidents — a kind of agreed list of dangers, such as out-of-control models or terrorists using AI for cyberattacks or bioweapons. Xi said the two nations have 'the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good.'

Taiwan and Iran may be linked. A senior U.S. official told Schifrin that Americans have died in Iranian attacks in the Middle East as a result of Chinese actions. Last year, the Trump administration authorized the largest-ever arms package to Taiwan and previewed a second. That second package has not been announced. The official acknowledged Beijing raised the possibility of canceling the summits if it were. But the main reason, the official said, is that the U.S. believes sending more weapons to Taiwan would lead China to send more weapons to Iran — a risk the U.S. does not want during the war with Iran.

Overall, both sides appear interested in stability.
why_it_matters: Trade truces, chip export rules and arms sales decided in rooms like this one ripple through global supply chains, jobs and the risk of war — including the danger of a crisis over Taiwan. Understanding what was actually agreed, and what was quietly shelved, matters far more than the ceremony.

Rules that stop certain products or technology from being sold to another country.

background_read: Xi Jinping (China's president and head of the Communist Party since 2013) has made managing relations with Washington a central goal, while Trump tends to treat diplomacy as a series of deals to be negotiated. The four-item agenda in the article comes from Nick Schifrin (a foreign affairs correspondent for the PBS NewsHour, an American public-television evening news programme).

Taiwan (a self-governing island off China's coast that Beijing claims as its own territory) is the most sensitive issue between the two countries. Since 1979 the United States has formally recognised Beijing while still selling Taiwan defensive weapons under the Taiwan Relations Act, a law passed by Congress that year — and every president since has had to balance those two commitments.

Rare earths (a group of metallic elements used in powerful magnets, batteries and electronics) are a Chinese strength, because China mines and processes most of the world's supply. They end up in ordinary phones and electric cars as well as military equipment such as the F-35 (a U.S. stealth fighter jet) mentioned in the article.

Semiconductors — the tiny chips that run computers, phones and weapons — are the other pressure point. The United States has restricted exports of advanced chips and chipmaking tools to China in recent years, and Beijing wants those controls eased.

American officials also worry about Iran, with which the United States has been in conflict. The article describes a U.S. fear that sending more weapons to Taiwan could lead China to send more weapons to Iran.

OPEN QUESTION: does a shared interest in stability produce real agreements?

perspectives.description: The extension of the trade truce, continued flows of rare earth magnets and the launch of an AI Dialogue all reduce the chance of an economic shock for ordinary consumers and businesses. Supporters argue that simply keeping the two governments talking about AI safety and trade is a genuine win, given how easily the relationship could spiral.

Critics note that Washington refused to ease semiconductor export controls and left the second Taiwan arms package unannounced, so little was actually given up. The new AI hotline is only a channel for reporting incidents, not an agreement with enforceable limits, which sceptics say leaves the biggest dangers unmanaged.

Analysts are struck by the way the article ties two very different disputes together: weapons for Taiwan and weapons reaching Iran. That kind of linkage is a classic bargaining move, but it also shows how easily regional conflicts become tangled in one giant negotiation between great powers.

The next big test is whether the withheld Taiwan arms package is ever announced, and whether the AI Dialogue produces real safeguards rather than just meetings. Meanwhile, China's near monopoly on rare earths gives Beijing leverage that could reappear in the next round of talks.
